newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh leader walks tightrope at home and abroad.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh leader walks tightrope at home and abroad.

text.p: Walking a political tightrope both at home and abroad, Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev is risking the wrath of an impoverished population and of powerful neighbour Russia.
Nazarbayev in recent weeks has dropped his customary caution in relations with Russia and is wading into the oil-rich country's economic reform programme.

But the new-found confidence of Nazarbayev, whose strong executive powers give him a tight hold on the former Soviet republic, risks provoking Russian ire and threatens Kazakhstan's hard-won market reforms, commentators say.
"Nazarbayev is a master at this four dimensional chess," said a foreign businessman and veteran observer of Kazakhstan's murky political scene.

"But with the divide between a super-rich elite and a poor majority, Nazarbayev faces a real challange in finding a place for a large amount of educated but effectively disenfranchised people," he said.

Anxious to halt his waning popularity, Nazarbayev, 57, told his government in the spring to find 36 billion tenge ($480 million) to pay off pension arrears by the end of the year or check in their Mercedes limousines, clear their desks and quit.
"He's already placing himself for the elections in 2000," said a Western diplomat based in Almaty. "Not that there's any real alternative to him right now."

With bonuses rolling in from quick-fire privatisations of the republic's oil and gas sector and a Eurobond issue later this year, Nazarbayev can pay the arrears without sparking inflation, said an international finance source in Almaty.
"But the president's men, seeing inflation down and some growth this year, are beginning to relax and go back to their old habits," he said.
The republic's ex-Communist Party chief, Nazarbayev is seen as having little grasp of market economics.

Investors have been alarmed by a decree requisitioning fuel for Kazakhstan's desperate farmers from private oil companies in return for dubious grain futures and a law making private banks invest part of their portfolios in small businesses.

Anti-market lapses like those nearly cost Kazakhstan a $446 million loan from the International Monetary Fund last month when the government tried to introduce a set of tax breaks which one observer called "institutionalised corruption".

Under pressure from foreign businessmen, Nazarbayev, who once said he learned as a Soviet bureaucrat "how to fake economic data, how to cheat, how to count each cow several times over", has promised to crack down on corruption.
But few investors see any improvement while the majority of the population view the government as deeply corrupt.
"These guys just can't get enough," said one exasperated oil executive.
The former steelworker Nazarbayev has also dropped his softly-softly approach to Russia, a sign he is more confident about his republic's independence.

He slapped down Russian allegations that a U.S. plane was spying, saying it had been called in to provide information on decades of environmental damage caused by Soviet nuclear tests, information which he accused Moscow of sitting on.

Fearful of unrest in northern Kazakhstan -- where much of the country's industry and agriculture is located but populated by mostly ethnic Russians -- Nazarbayev slammed Russian Cossack units patrolling the border as "highwaymen".
Nazarbayev is looking to other neighbours, especially China which recently won a major oil concession, for alternative routes for trade and transport.

The United States, with a major strategic interest both in Kazakh oil and the country's independence from Russia, gives strong backing to Nazarbayev. But landlocked Kazakhstan remains heavily dependent on Russia for exports of its oil and gas.
"In that light, his statements in recent weeks have been surprising," said the diplomat.
